answers: The phonological similarity effect is the finding that people recall a list worse when its items sound alike than when they sound different. What makes it striking is that it still happens when people read the items silently, with no sound at all. That tells us the sound is what matters, which is why acoustic similarity effect is arguably the better name.

What was manipulated there was whether people kept their speech-based recoding available. On some trials they said one, two, three, four out loud over and over, which is articulatory suppression, and on others they stayed quiet. Suppression keeps the articulatory control process busy, so visual items cannot be recoded into speech, and then sound-alike and sound-different lists were recalled equally well.

This is an example of a phonological code, meaning a speech-based form of the items. If memory held only a visual code, the mix-ups would be between letters that look alike, such as E and F. Because sound-alike letters are the ones recalled worse, even when read silently, people must be recoding what they see into speech.

Roodenrys and colleagues (2002) found that in short-term memory tasks, words from large neighborhoods are recalled better than words from small neighborhoods. People saw a sequence of words and then gave them back in order, and a word like cat did better than a word like hippopotamus. So what a person knows about the language helps them hold words briefly.

A word's neighborhood is every word you can make by changing one letter, which is the orthographic neighborhood, or one sound, which is the phonological neighborhood. Cat has many neighbors, such as bat, cot and can, so it is a large neighborhood word. Hippopotamus has none, so it is a small neighborhood word.

Memory span is not a pure measure of short-term capacity because long-term memory affects it. Roodenrys and colleagues (2002) showed that words with many neighbors are recalled better, so knowledge stored in long-term memory changes short-term performance. If span depends partly on what you already know, it cannot be telling you only about short-term capacity.

Peterson and Peterson (1959) concluded that short-term memory holds information only briefly, and that without rehearsal it is lost through decay. The longer people counted backwards before recall, the less likely they were to remember the letters. Because counting backwards is so different from remembering letters, they judged interference an unlikely cause. Decay is their own conclusion, and the results have also been given an alternative explanation.

What was manipulated was how long people did a distractor task before they had to recall. People saw three consonants, then a number, and counted backwards out loud by threes for several seconds. The counting stopped them from rehearsing the letters, and the length of that delay was what varied. Recall got worse as the delay got longer.

That is decay, meaning information fades from short-term memory over time unless it is rehearsed. In the Brown-Peterson task, recall dropped the longer the counting lasted, with rehearsal blocked. Peterson and Peterson (1959) took that as decay, since time passing was the thing that mattered and the counting task was too different from the letters to interfere.

The modality effect is better memory for the last one or two items of a list when the list is heard than when it is read silently. It is about those final items, not the whole list. It also shows up for lists that are lip-read or silently mouthed, so it is not only about hearing.

The comparison was between lists that were heard and lists that were read silently. People either heard or saw the digits one through nine in a random order and then gave them back in the order presented. Half the trials were auditory and half were visual, and the difference showed up in memory for the last items.

Neath and Surprenant (2003) favor the idea that hearing provides an additional type of information compared with reading. When you recall the last items of a list, you do better if you also have information about how the list sounded. That extra sound information is what gives the heard lists their advantage at the end.

Sperling (1960) found that when the cue came right after the display disappeared, observers reported the cued part almost perfectly, whichever part it was. That means a sensory, or iconic, store briefly held nearly a complete copy of the display. The usual small amount people report comes from the time needed to report, not from what they saw.

What was manipulated was when the cue arrived. A grid of letters flashed very briefly, and then a tone told the observer which row to report, with the tone coming either right away or after a delay. With a delayed cue, performance fell back toward the usual limit, which shows how briefly the store lasts.

That is the sensory, or iconic, store, a very brief store of raw, unanalyzed input. In Sperling's (1960) partial report, an immediate cue let people report the cued row almost perfectly, so the store must have held nearly all of the display. It fades very fast, which is why a delayed cue lost most of the advantage.

The position error effect is the finding that when we remember a list, order mistakes are systematic and not random. Most of the time an item is recalled in its correct position. When a mistake does happen, the item usually comes out close to where it belongs, so forgetting a position is not the same as losing the item.

Misplaced items usually end up in an adjacent position. The third item is more likely to show up second or fourth than first or last, and rarely far from where it really belongs. So the errors are patterned, and people still remember roughly where each item went, even when they get the exact spot wrong.

Percent correct alone makes forgetting look like lost information. A response that is one place off counts as simply wrong, even though the person still knows roughly where the item belonged. Looking at where each recalled item was placed shows that approximate position information is kept, and percent correct hides that.

Shepard and Metzler (1971) found that the larger the turn between two block shapes, the longer people took to respond, and the extra time grew at a constant rate. People were judging whether the shapes were the same or mirror images. Rotating a mental image takes time, just as turning a real object does, which suggests mental images are much like real images.

What was manipulated was how much one block shape was turned relative to the other. The two shapes appeared side by side, either identical or mirror images, rotated by different angles. People judged same or different as quickly as possible, and their reaction time was recorded. Reaction time rose with the size of the turn.

Descriptions of mental images are unreliable, so researchers cannot trust what people say about their images. Instead they use tasks that require imagery and vary one critical part of the task. That lets them work out objectively what images are like, which is what Shepard and Metzler (1971) did by varying how far one block shape was turned.

Tversky and Kahneman (1983) showed that people's estimates of probability often differ greatly from objective probability. A striking example is the conjunction fallacy, judging that A and B together are more likely than A alone or B alone. By the rules of probability a combination can never be more likely than either part alone, so these judgments point to heuristics, which trade accuracy for speed.

Shafir, Smith and Osherson (1990) had people read short descriptions of a person and rate how likely it was that the person had certain professions or took part in certain activities. People sometimes rated the combination as more likely than one part of it. That points to reliance on heuristics rather than the rules of probability.

That is the conjunction fallacy. Judging A and B together as more likely than A alone breaks the rules of probability, because a combination can never be more likely than either part on its own. It shows that people use heuristics, which are usually good enough day to day but can lead to incorrect judgments.

The best cards are D and 7, because those are the ones that could show the rule is broken. A D without a 3 would falsify the rule, and so would a 7 with a D behind it. Most people pick D and 3, but the 3 can only confirm the rule, since the rule says nothing about what must be behind a 3.

Wason and Shapiro (1971) compared abstract rules, made of letters and numbers, with thematic rules, like borrowing a car. People saw a rule and four cards and chose the two cards to turn over to see if the rule was true. Thematic rules were much easier, while on the abstract rule most people chose D and 3 instead of D and 7.

Because it uses familiar content, so people can draw on relevant experience. The right cards are the borrowed car and the empty gas tank, because those could reveal someone who borrowed the car and did not fill it. With an abstract rule, people have to rely solely on logic, and that is much harder.

A framing effect is when the perceived context or wording of a choice makes a big difference, even when the situations are otherwise equivalent. The same choice can be presented in two different ways, and people choose differently depending on the version. The choice follows the framing and not the substance.

In classic framing research, as summarized by Kahneman and Tversky (1982), the same choice was presented in two different ways, with gain wording or with loss wording. People read situations and chose between two options, in one of two question sets that framed the same choices differently. Their choices depended on which wording they saw.

That is a framing effect. Gain wording typically pushes people toward the sure option, while loss wording pushes them toward the gamble. The situations are otherwise equivalent, so the fact that the choice changes with the wording shows that decisions are shaped by how a choice is framed and not only by what the options are.

You should switch, because switching wins about two-thirds of the time and staying wins only about one-third. Your first pick has a one in three chance of being right, so there is a two in three chance the prize is behind one of the other two doors. When the host opens an empty door, that whole two in three moves to the remaining door.

The mistake is treating the two remaining doors as equally likely. It feels like a fifty-fifty choice, which is why many people think it does not matter whether they stay or switch. That intuition is incorrect, because your own door stays at one in three while the other door now carries two in three.

The first pick keeps a one in three chance of being right. Opening a no-prize door does not change that, so your door stays at one in three. The other two in three chance is what moves to the remaining door, and that is why switching is the better choice.

With gains, people typically avoid risk and take the sure thing. When the choice is about something they stand to win, a guaranteed outcome is preferred over a gamble, even when the gamble has a stated chance of winning more. This is the gain side of how risky choices depend on how outcomes are perceived, not only on the objective odds.

With losses, people typically seek risk and take the gamble. When the sure outcome is a loss, they are more willing to gamble than to accept it, hoping to avoid the loss altogether. So losses lead to gambling, not caution, and this is the loss side of how risky choices depend on how outcomes are perceived.

What was varied was whether the guaranteed outcome was a gain or a loss, with a gamble as the alternative. People played a wheel-of-fortune game with a stated chance of winning and losing if they gambled, and a stated amount guaranteed if they did not. That showed risky decisions depend on how outcomes are perceived, not just on the objective odds.

answers.topic: German & Defeyter (2000): Immunity to functional fixedness in young children
answers: German and Defeyter (2000) found that 5-year-olds were immune to functional fixedness. They were not slowed by having seen the box as a container, and they were even faster than the older children in that condition. So the younger children did better here, not worse, which is the opposite of what you might expect since problem solving normally improves with age.

German and Defeyter (2000) manipulated whether the box had first been shown as a container, which is preutilization. Children aged 5, 6 and 7 helped a toy bear reach a toy on a high shelf, and the solution was to turn the box over and use it as a support. In one condition the other objects started inside the box, and in the other they sat beside it. Time to offer the box solution was measured.

That is functional fixedness, being stuck on an object's usual function, so that a new use is slow or missed. The 6- and 7-year-olds were slower to use the box as a support after seeing it as a container. The authors explained this by saying younger children have a more fluid idea of function, while older children hold it more rigidly and must restructure it.

answers.topic: Leist et al. (2022): Irrelevant speech impairs serial recall of verbal but not spatial items
answers: Leist and colleagues (2022) found that irrelevant speech did not impair spatial recall. It impaired verbal recall but not spatial recall, in both third-grade children and adults. So the effect is specific to verbal material. That is hard for the attention-capture and changing-state accounts, which predict disruption of spatial items too, and it fits similarity-based interference with phonological representations.

Leist and colleagues (2022) varied the type of item, the speech people heard, and the age group. Items were either verbal, pictured objects, or spatial, dot locations. People heard quiet, a repeated syllable, which is steady-state, or different syllables, which is changing-state, and were told to ignore it. Third graders and adults were tested, and they had to recall the order of the items.

That is the irrelevant speech effect, which is that speech you are told to ignore impairs serial recall. Changing-state speech, with different syllables, hurts more than steady-state speech, with one syllable repeated. Leist and colleagues (2022) found it happened for verbal items only, which points to interference with phonological representations.

answers.topic: Morrison & Richmond (2020): Offloading items from memory
answers: Morrison and Richmond (2020) found that offloading improved memory, especially at high loads, meaning the longer lists. People also offloaded more as the load rose. So having pen and paper to write things down helped most exactly when the memory demands were highest, and people used it more when they needed it.

Morrison and Richmond (2020) compared a no-choice block, where people relied on memory alone, with a choice block, where they had pen and paper and could write anything down if they wished. Students heard lists of letters of different lengths and said them back in order. They also completed working memory span tasks to measure their capacity.

No, memory ability did not predict who offloaded, and capacity did not predict the benefit either. The researchers had expected people with lower working memory capacity to offload more. Instead, offloading may be a compensatory strategy that helps across a wide range of memory ability.

Hoover and Healy (2019) found that incorrect reasoners mostly recalled and recognized the phrase more than, so it was not simply overlooked. They apparently did not use its meaning. Some reasoners did lose the phrase and many stayed very confident, so substitution may still occur for some people.

Hoover and Healy (2019) compared a standard bat-and-ball problem containing more than with a control version without it. People answered each version and rated their confidence, and later were asked to recall the problem and recognize its wording. Simple math problems were placed in between as interference for most participants.

Because they cannot be sure the error was unconscious attribute substitution, where people neglect more than and answer an easier question. Since the wrong reasoners mostly remembered the phrase, Hoover and Healy (2019) cannot confirm substitution as the cause. They prefer the term error sensitivity, which only says people notice they may be wrong.

answers.topic: Giuliani et al. (2023): The joint effect of framing and defaults on choice behavior
answers: Giuliani and colleagues (2023) found that a risky default raised risk taking. A sure default, however, did not raise risk aversion. So a preselected option pushed people toward risk when the default was the gamble, but not toward caution when the default was the sure thing.

Giuliani and colleagues (2023) varied the wording, gain or loss, and the default, which was none, a sure default or a risky default. Each person was randomly assigned to one of the conditions and chose in a life-or-death scenario and a money scenario involving their own money. They chose between a sure option and a risky one.

Giuliani and colleagues (2023) found that the framing effect and the default effect were additive. They found a classic framing effect, and a risky default raised risk taking on top of it. Afterward, people who thought the default was the most rational choice followed it most, though that question came after the choice, so it may partly be a justification.

answers.topic: Chein et al. (2011) and Albert, Chein & Steinberg (2013): Peers and the adolescent brain
answers: Chein and colleagues (2011) found that adolescents took significantly more risks in the driving game when friends were watching. Reward-related regions, the ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex, were more active in adolescents when peers watched, and this went with risky decisions. The age-by-context difference on behavior was not itself significant in this small sample.

The cognitive-control regions did not change with peers. Whether friends were watching or not, those regions stayed the same, so the peer context did not alter them. Chein and colleagues (2011) therefore concluded that the peer effect works mainly through reward circuitry, not through weaker reasoning, though the two systems may interact.

Albert, Chein and Steinberg (2013) say it is the peer context. Adolescents reason about risk as well as adults in the lab, but with peers present they take more risks and adults do not. Peers prime the reward system while the cognitive-control system matures slowly, and that maturational gap raises risk taking.

notes: Modality effect and Monty Hall and Position Error Effect cards list no researcher in the material, so those answers cite none except Neath and Surprenant (2003) where the question asks.
Peterson and Peterson (1959) is given in the material as concluding decay, with the results also having an alternative explanation; the answer records decay as the researchers' own conclusion.

Chein et al. (2011): the material notes the age-by-context difference on behavior was not itself significant in the small sample; the answers say adolescents took more risks when watched, as the material does, without claiming a significant interaction.
Giuliani et al. (2023): the rationality-belief question came after the choice and was exploratory, so the answer flags it as possibly a justification.
The Wason answer on the car rule uses the material's wording, borrowed car and empty gas tank cards; the question text mentions car and gas tank, matching the material.
